blocks.text: Belon writes that in Egypt he saw the whole preserved bodies of certain winged serpents which have feet and are said to fly from Arabia into Egypt, Observations book 2, ch. 70, p. 133 (in the Sylloge Itinerarior. edited by Paulus, vol. 1, p. 238). But one should read what a certain learned man has remarked on that passage of Belon in the Notarum Mantissa appended to the second part of the said Sylloge, p. 264. Compare also our note 2 below.

Oedmann, Vermischte Sammlungen fasc. 6, ch. 7, p. 71 ff., has collected the reports of others on winged serpents. He rightly points out, however, that the serpents flying with membranous wings of which ancient and more recent writers speak are flying lizards, [III, 215] which Linnaeus (Syst. Nat. vol. 1, part 3, p. 1056, 13th ed.) calls dracones [dragons], and who in the Amoenitt. Academm. fasc. 1, p. 126, also described the Lacerta cauda tereti, pedibus pentadactylis, alis femore connexis, crista gulae triplici [lizard with a rounded tail, five-toed feet, wings joined to the thigh, and a threefold crest on the throat]. — Michaelis, in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. vol. 6, p. 2353, sees here too his cerastes or regulus, interpreting the name שרף as noble or prince, comparing the Arabic شرف [sharufa], he was noble. He thinks the name prince was given to the cerastes from the horns or feelers that distinguish this kind of serpent, which seemed to present the appearance of a crown. So in Michaelis' opinion the cerastes bore three names among the Hebrews: 1. צפע, 2. שפיפון, 3. שרף. But he confuses the coronella with the cerastes; see our note 1 above on the preceding Chapter. We, however, have seen that only שפיפון is the cerastes cornutus, and צפע the coronella petola; while that שרף is to be referred to the dracones or flying lizards is suggested by the passages Es. XIV, 29. XXX, 6., where the שרף is expressly called flying or winged, מעופף. As for Michaelis' referring our שרף to the Arabic شرف [sharufa], he was noble, he seems not to have observed the usage of the verb שרף among the Hebrews, which always occurs solely in the sense of burning.
